questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Identify the defining feature of an enlightened despot
questions.stem: Which ruler is commonly cited as an enlightened despot who reformed laws while keeping absolute power?

options.text: Frederick the Great of Prussia who codified laws and promoted education
Louis XVI of France who convened the Estates-General in 1789
options.misconception: confuses a reforming absolute monarch with a constitutional one

options.text: Napoleon Bonaparte who crowned himself emperor after the revolution
options.misconception: mistakes a post-revolutionary emperor for an enlightened despot

options.text: Charles I of England who clashed with Parliament over divine right
options.misconception: confuses an absolutist martyr with an enlightened reformer

questions.explanation: Frederick the Great combined absolute rule with legal and educational reforms. The others either faced constitutional limits or rose after the Enlightenment's peak.
questions.hint: Look for a ruler who kept power yet reformed laws.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the Glorious Revolution produced a constitutional settlement
questions.stem: Why did the settlement after 1688 limit the English monarch while preserving the throne?

answer.exemplar: The settlement removed James II and invited William and Mary under conditions that required parliamentary consent for taxation and lawmaking, keeping the crown but making it accountable to Parliament rather than to divine right alone.

questions.explanation: The settlement balanced legitimacy and constraint by tying the crown to parliamentary authority. It avoided both republican rule and unchecked absolutism.
questions.hint: Think about who granted the crown and on what terms.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Define constitutionalism in contrast to absolutism

stimulus.body: A government is most free when its powers are limited by fundamental law. Where one person rules by personal will alone, no subject can be secure in property or conscience. Lasting order therefore rests on written rules that bind rulers and ruled alike.

questions.stem: Based on this excerpt, what does the author treat as the foundation of lasting political order?

options.text: The personal virtue and wisdom of a single enlightened ruler
options.misconception: reads the passage as praising enlightened absolutism

options.text: Military strength that deters rebellion and enforces obedience
options.misconception: imports a Hobbesian fear argument not stated here

options.text: Written fundamental laws that bind both rulers and subjects
Popular consent expressed through frequent elections and parties
options.misconception: adds modern democratic machinery absent from the excerpt

questions.explanation: The excerpt argues that order rests on written rules binding rulers and ruled. It rejects rule by personal will and does not invoke elections or force.
questions.hint: Notice the phrase about rules binding both sides.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Compare alternatives to absolutism in early modern Europe
questions.stem: Which alternative to absolutism best combined popular participation with strong executive stability in the eighteenth century?

options.text: A republic with annual elections and no hereditary executive
options.misconception: assumes frequent elections alone ensured stability

options.text: A military dictatorship suspending all civilian institutions
options.misconception: mistakes emergency rule for a durable alternative

options.text: A theocratic council ruling by divine revelation and scripture
options.misconception: confuses religious authority with constitutional balance

options.text: A mixed constitution balancing monarchy, aristocracy, and commons

questions.explanation: The mixed constitution was praised for blending participation and stability. Pure republics risked instability, theocracies lacked balance, and dictatorships were not durable alternatives.
questions.hint: Think of the model praised by Montesquieu and English writers.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Identify a key claim of social contract theory
questions.stem: In social contract theory, what gives a government legitimate authority over its people?

options.text: The consent of the governed through a collective agreement
Divine appointment of a hereditary monarch by religious sanction
options.misconception: confuses divine right with consent-based legitimacy

options.text: Conquest and the superior force of a victorious army
options.misconception: mistakes Hobbesian power for legitimate authority

options.text: Hereditary privilege passed down through noble bloodlines
options.misconception: confuses aristocratic tradition with contractual consent

questions.explanation: Social contract theory grounds authority in consent. Divine right, conquest, and bloodline are rival theories that contract thinkers rejected.
questions.hint: Look for the idea of agreement among the people.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate absolutism against its stated goals
questions.stem: Why might an eighteenth-century observer judge absolutism a success in one country but a failure in another?

answer.exemplar: An observer might praise absolutism where it delivered legal reform, religious toleration, and efficient administration, yet condemn it where it produced arbitrary taxation, censorship, and stagnant institutions without accountability.

questions.explanation: Judgments depended on outcomes and on whether reform served subjects or only the crown. Absolutism lacked mechanisms to correct failures.
questions.hint: Consider what reforms were delivered and who benefited.

One embraced religious toleration while the other enforced orthodoxy

questions.explanation: The source contrasts parliamentary negotiation with centralized lawmaking. Military, social, and religious claims are not raised in the excerpt.
questions.hint: Match the wording about negotiation and centralization.

questions.learningObjective: Identify an Enlightenment argument against divine right
questions.stem: Which Enlightenment argument most directly undermined the claim that monarchs rule by divine right?

options.text: Kings derive authority from ancestral bloodlines and noble birth
options.misconception: restates the very doctrine being challenged

options.text: Religious institutions should appoint rulers to maintain harmony
options.misconception: confuses clerical authority with Enlightenment reason

options.text: Tradition and custom provide the safest guide to political order
options.misconception: appeals to conservatism rather than Enlightenment critique

options.text: All humans share natural reason, so no person is born to command others

questions.explanation: Enlightenment thinkers used natural equality and shared reason to challenge divine right. Bloodline, tradition, and clerical appointment support rather than undermine it.

questions.learningObjective: Recognize limits of reforms imposed from above
questions.stem: What was a common limit of reforms enacted by enlightened despots without popular consent?

options.text: They often lacked enforcement or popular buy-in beyond the court
They were always reversed by the next ruler within a single year
options.misconception: overstates the speed and certainty of reversal

options.text: They were written only in Latin and never translated locally

questions.explanation: Reforms from above often failed to reach local practice without popular support. Reversal was not always immediate, and unanimous consent was not required.
questions.hint: Think about enforcement and public support.

answer.exemplar: Salons gathered thinkers, writers, and nobles to debate new ideas, while pamphlets, journals, and books carried those debates to merchants, professionals, and the wider literate public across borders.

questions.explanation: Personal networks and print worked together to circulate ideas. Neither alone reached as far as both combined.
questions.hint: Combine social gathering with printed circulation.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Compare Locke and Hobbes on the state of nature

stimulus.body: In one account, the state of nature is a war of all against all, so only an absolute sovereign can secure peace. In another, people already possess natural rights to life and property, and government exists to protect them, with resistance justified when it fails.

questions.stem: Which thinker matches the second account in this source?

options.text: Hobbes, who argued for an absolute sovereign to end chaos
options.misconception: assigns the first account to the wrong thinker

options.text: Rousseau, who located sovereignty in the general will
options.misconception: imports a later thinker not described here

options.text: Locke, who grounded government in protecting natural rights
Montesquieu, who separated powers into distinct branches
options.misconception: confuses institutional design with contract theory

questions.explanation: The second account protects natural rights and permits resistance, matching Locke. Hobbes matches the first; Rousseau and Montesquieu are different theories.
questions.hint: Match rights, protection, and justified resistance.

options.text: The extent of legal and educational reform benefiting subjects

questions.explanation: Enlightenment in an absolutist context meant reforms benefiting subjects. Army size, reign length, and alliances are not decisive measures.
questions.hint: Look for reforms that served the people.
